content: Sleep paralysis is a condition in which an individual experiences temporary paralysis of the body either shortly after waking up (referred to as hypnopompic paralysis) or, less commonly, just before falling asleep (referred to as hypnagogic paralysis). This phenomenon is closely linked to the natural paralysis that occurs during REM (rapid eye movement) sleep, known as REM atonia. In cases of sleep paralysis, the brain transitions out of the REM state, but the body remains paralyzed. This results in the affected person being fully conscious but unable to move. During these episodes, individuals may also experience hypnagogic hallucinations, which can involve vivid sensory perceptions. These hallucinations, combined with the inability to move, often lead people to believe they are dreaming. This explains why many individuals describe dreams in which they feel frozen or unable to move. The hallucinatory aspect of sleep paralysis can further reinforce the perception that the experience is dream-like, as fantastical or surreal objects may appear in the environment alongside normal visual input. The primary symptom of sleep paralysis is the inability to move or speak, despite being fully aware, during the transition into or out of sleep. This paralysis can be partial or complete and is often accompanied by hypnagogic hallucinations, which may be auditory, tactile, or visual in nature. Affected individuals may also experience difficulty breathing, as if a heavy weight is pressing on their chest. This sensation, combined with the hallucinations, can evoke feelings of fear and the perception of an evil presence, such as a witch, which has led to the term Old Hag Syndrome. If a polysomnographic study is conducted during an episode, it may reveal one or more of the following: suppression of skeletal muscle tone, REM sleep occurring at the onset of sleep, or dissociated REM sleep. The paralysis typically lasts for a few seconds to a few minutes before the individual either returns to REM sleep or fully awakens. If the person re-enters REM sleep while remaining conscious, they may enter a lucid dreaming state. The exact physiological mechanisms underlying sleep paralysis are not fully understood. However, it is believed to involve the inhibition of motor neurons in the pons region of the brain. Low levels of melatonin may also play a role by disrupting the depolarization current in nerves, thereby preventing muscle stimulation. This mechanism is thought to prevent the body from physically enacting movements associated with dreams, such as running or flailing. Sleep paralysis is more common in individuals with narcolepsy, but studies suggest that most people will experience it at least once or twice in their lifetime. Several factors are known to increase the likelihood of sleep paralysis and associated hallucinations. These include sleeping in a supine position (lying on the back), irregular sleep schedules (e.g., naps, sleep deprivation, or oversleeping), heightened stress levels, sudden changes in environment or lifestyle, and preceding lucid dreams. Additionally, the conscious induction of sleep paralysis is a technique used by some individuals to enter a lucid dreaming state, known as wake-initiated lucid dreaming (WILD). The use of artificial sleep aids, medications for attention deficit disorder (ADD), antihistamines, or hallucinogenic drugs may also increase the risk of sleep paralysis. During an episode of sleep paralysis, individuals may be advised to attempt moving their facial muscles or shifting their eyes from side to side, as these actions may help terminate the episode more quickly. Pharmacological treatment options include clonazepam, which has been shown to be highly effective. The initial recommended dose is 0.5 mg at bedtime, with the possibility of increasing to 1 mg per night if necessary. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as fluoxetine, have also been reported to reduce the frequency of sleep paralysis episodes in some individuals, although the effects are not consistent across all patients. Cultural interpretations of sleep paralysis vary widely. In Japan, it is referred to as kanashibari, meaning bound or fastened in metal. In Hungarian folklore, it is called lidércnyomás, attributed to supernatural entities such as witches or fairies. Kurdish people describe it as mottaka, believing it to be caused by a ghost or evil spirit. In New Guinea, it is associated with sacred trees that feed on human essence during the night. In Turkey, it is called karabasan, believed to be caused by a creature attacking during sleep. In Mexico, it is referred to as se me subió el muerto, meaning the dead person got on me. Among the Yoruba people of Nigeria, it is known as ogun oru, or nocturnal warfare, attributed to demonic infiltration during dreams. African-American communities often describe it as the witch is riding you or the haint is riding you, and studies suggest a predisposition to isolated sleep paralysis in this population, particularly among those who experience frequent episodes. Sleep paralysis has also been referenced in literature, art, and music. For example, Miguel de Cervantes mentions it in Don Quixote (1605), and Herman Melville describes it in Moby-Dick (1851). Ernest Hemingway's The Snows of Kilimanjaro (1936) includes an account of the phenomenon, as does Kingsley Amis' The Green Man (1969). Maxine Hong Kingston recounts an episode in The Woman Warrior (1975), and the progressive rock band Dredg explores the topic in their album El Cielo (2001). Other cultural and artistic references further highlight the widespread recognition of this condition across different societies and time periods.
